div.p: ergy efficiency metrics for real-time systems, numerous algorithms have been proposed to construct synthetic tasksets for simulation. The resulting taskset characteristics should ideally reflect real workloads while the algorithms generating these tasksets should be efficient. Any experimentation using these tasksets will highly depend on their properties. Current approaches construct the sets by choosing taskset periods and utilisation from statistical distributions and compute the task worst case execution times accordingly. Tasks are generated through timed loops or matrix operations up to the specified task WCET. At times, the taskset hyper-period is bounded to minimise simulation interval through selected assignment of task periods. However, tasks which burn processor cycles through loops and matrix operations do not always reflect realistic task loads. In this paper, we propose a methodology for generating realistic tasksets based on available embedded benchmarks. We extend on previous work and propose new algorithms: CPA-AU/DU (Compute-Propagate-Adjust Ascending/Descending Utilisation) which efficiently pair taskset WCETs with selected discrete periods. Our tasksets have bounded and feasible simulation interval and meet desired total utilisation with minimum digression errors. We also show that our algorithms run in polynomial time.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time embedded systems are pervasive in industrial and commercial applications. The demands for high reliability and energy efficiency elicit the need for developing fault-tolerant, energy (and thermally-) aware schedulers while meeting schedulabilty constraints. The ubiquitous use of homogeneous and heterogeneous multi-core embedded systems adds further dimensions of complexity in developing and testing new task allocation, scheduling and core activation algorithms. To evaluate the performance of newly developed solutions, most of the scientific literature has heavily relied on simulators with a priori knowledge of the target processor. These processor models are often simplified to a certain degree due to the inherent complexity of the hardware or lack of disclosure of design and timing specifications. Moreover, the simulation correctness and faithfulness in representing realworld applications is dependant on the taskset properties. For example, a taskset represented by the timing parameters of its individual tasks might be sufficient in simulating feasibility of scheduling algorithms. However, it offers no insights into the instruction makeup of each task, and consequently its cache access behaviour, blocking or interaction with other tasks in the system. Such insights might be consequential in assess-ing reliability and energy-efficiency of real-time algorithms. For example, the work of Saha and Ravindran [1] revealed numerous inconsistencies between reported energy savings in literature simulations and those carried on hardware platforms.

In preparing tasksets, the methodology most widely used in literature starts with computing task utilisations. Given a desired total taskset utilisation, individual task utilsations are generated whose sum equal the desired total. Efficient, independent and unbiased algorithms have been proposed. For uniprocessor systems, the UUniFast algorithms [2] is usually used. For the multiprocessor domain, the UUniFast algorithm has been extended into UUniFast-Discard Algorithm [3]. UUniFast-Discard basically applies UUniFast algorithm and discards any unfeasible solutions. For a certain number of tasks and desired total utilisation, the high discard ratio renders the algorithm inefficient. Randfixedsum algorithm [4] addresses the shortcomings of UUniFast-Discard and works for any number of tasks n and total utilisation U .

Task periods are generated independent from task utilisation computations. Periods are chosen from a statistical distribution (e.g. uniform, log-uniform, bi-modal) such that they fall within certain time bands (i.e. 10ms -1000ms). Once the task utilisation and periods are known, the task worst case execution times are then computed according to Eq. 1. Task deadline and priorities assignment follow (i.e. in case of fixed priority systems). If the taskset is to be used in discrete time/event simulations, the WCETs could are rounded. Alternatively, the simulator base time unit is adjusted (e.g. decreasing it from ms to µs). The hyper-period is computed as the least common multiple of all task periods in the dataset. Total simulation interval is directly related to the hyper-period [5]. Notable approaches to minimise the hyper-period are based on generating harmonic periods [6], [7], [8].

Should the simulation be conducted in software simulators (e.g. discrete event/time simulators), then the resulting temporal parameters are sufficient to define the taskset. However, if the taskset is to be run on real hardware platforms or emulators, the tasks are to be synthetically constructed. In one approach, [9], [10], [11], [1], each task simply burns processor cycles through timed loops until the assigned task WCET is reached. A similar approach is also used in [12] for control applications on multi-core platforms. When memory and cache access behaviour is simulated, tasks are constructed with matrix operations [13]. Each task is programmed as one thread with its own address space. This approach is direct and simple, however; the underlying taskset might not capture the realistic behaviour of industrial and commercial workloads. Such synthetic sets potentially fail to simulate task interactions, I/O access and blocking, and in many cases cache behaviour.

A more realistic approach is to use embedded benchmark suites which reflect the typical behaviour of a variety of tasks in different embedded applications [14], [15]. However, the arising issue is that computing WCETs from the sets of discrete periods and computed utilisations is invalid. In this case, a more formal approach to estimate the WCET of the benchmark taskset needs to be carried out. This is a complex and rigorous task and perhaps the reason why the literature has relied on the aforementioned simpler approaches for so long.

div.head: A. Problem Statement and Contributions
div.p: The classical methodology to prepare tasksets is simple and straightforward. Algorithms exist to generate task utilisations and task periods. Eq. 1 is applied to compute the tasks worst case execution times. Despite that we make use of the same randfixedsum algorithm to generate task utilisations, our methodology demands that the first step be estimating the WCET of the benchmark suite. WCET estimation is regarded as a complex and costly assignment. Furthermore, applying Eq. 1 to obtain the task periods does not directly work. We are restricted by the discrete period set which allows for a bounded hyper-period to limit simulation time. In consequence, two problems arise :

• Given both the task WCET and utilisation sets, how to select WCET-utilisation pairs such that the resulting period is as close as possible to one of the discrete periods in the hyper-period bounded set. • Since a discrete period is now selected, the task utilisation will henceforth change. Effectively, each task utilisation will change and the total desired utilisation will no longer be satisfied. We address all these issues in this paper. Our main contributions are summarised as follows:

• We propose a new methodology to build tasksets from realistic industrial benchmarks for a more realistic real-time system simulation on hardware platforms. We use measurement based probabilistic timing analysis techniques to estimate WCETs. • We practically show that any direct pairing approach between members of the estimated WCETs and discrete periods sets (using exhaustive or heuristic approaches) will frequently result in a total utilisation that diverges considerably from the desired utilisation. • We propose a set of feedback adaptive algorithms which pair the estimated WCETs with the discrete bounded periods. We show that the total utilisation of the final taskset converges to the desired total utilisation with minimal errors. We show that our algorithms run in polynomial time. In this paper, we present the system model in Section II. Some background on WCET estimation followed by our proposed algorithms are found in Section III. We detail the experimental setup in Section IV. We illustrate and discuss the results of our algorithms in Section V. We conclude with brief overview of the methodology and results in Section VI.

div.head: III. BACKGROUND AND PROPOSED ALGORITHMS
div.p: Estimating Worst Case Execution Times of real-time tasks is an arduous endeavour. To date, numerous techniques have been designed to find the upper-bounds of task execution time. The devised techniques largely fall under three approaches: static-based, measurement-based, and hybrid analysis. Each of the three approaches can be carried in either deterministic or probabilistic fashion. Static WCET estimaion is based on analysing the source code of the program and constructing a path-flow model. User annotation of the source code is often required (e.g. specify number of loop iterations) and requires in-depth knowledge of the program. The path flow is used in conjunction with a timing model of the target hardware platform to estimate WCETs. Many static WCET estimation tools are used in academia and industry [16], [17], [18], [19], however; the lack of support for many architectures especially modern and multicore processors, the tools cost, setup and analysis time for numerous tasks makes them less of an option.

Measurement based WCET estimation demands understanding of the task source code and potentially a large set of various inputs and initial conditions which include the path which leads to the WCET. This approach requires accurate measurements procedures in the sense that the tools used to measure the time are not intrusive and should not introduce measurement errors. Finally, given the collected measurements, there is no clear consensus on how the WCET is determined. A practical approach is to add a certain percentage to the highest measured execution time.

A novel approach which extends measurement based techniques through probabilistic analysis has been explored in [20]. This approach is formally called Measurement Based Probability Timing Analysis (MBPTA). The rationale behind adopting probabilistic WCET estimation (pWCET) is mainly the pitfalls of static WCET tools mentioned above. Measurement based techniques requires far more time and test patterns than their probabilistic counterparts. One way to conduct MBPTA is based on Extreme Value Theory (EVT). EVT is a branch of statistics which is mainly concerned with the tails (extremities) of a statistical distributions [20]. It is worth noting that the algorithms we propose in this paper are independent from the technique employed to estimate the WCET. It is left to the reader to select any WCET estimation techniques that is deemed fit. We detail our approach in estimating WCET using EVT in Section. IV. For a complete review of WCET estimation techniques, we refer the reader to [21].

div.head: A. Exhaustive Approach -PU Algorithm
div.p: Once the WCET values are estimated, a set of individual task utilisations is generated for a desired total utilisation. We construct a set of discrete periods that have a bounded hyperperiod to the end effect of limiting total simulation time.

One possibility to address the issues raised in Subsection I-A is using an exhaustive approach. An exhaustive approach permutes all possible WCET/Utilisation pairs. We explore this method as a reference point when tasksets are small (10). We name this algorithm Permuted Utilisation, or simply PU. We also use this algorithm to show that any algorithm regardless of its pairing approach will have a final summed utilisation with potentially high deviation errors. Since the exhaustive approach yielded on average high deviation errors (Section V), this was the motivation to introduce the CPA algorithm.

The CPA algorithm features continuous adaptive and feedback operations. The error difference between computed periods and the closest discrete periods is used as a feedback to select which WCET and utilisation to pair. Given the newly assigned discrete period and the ensuing new utilisation, the difference between the old and new utilisations is used to adjust the remaining utilisations. This adaptive procedure ensures that we keep as close as possible to the target utilisation as the algorithm moves forward and discrete periods and utilisations are paired. The details of the algorithm are detailed in the following subsection and the pseudo-code is listed in Algorithm 1.

div.head: B. Compute Propagate and Adjust Algorithms (CPA)
div.p: The CPA algorithm takes in the WCETs vector C and an equal-size vector of task utilisations U . The utilisations are ordered in ascending (CPA-AU), or descending order (CPA-DU). A discrete periods set H with a bounded hyper-period is generated according to [6]. In the Compute Phase, a period matrix P is computed per Eq. 1. Each task WCET C i is divided by each element in the utilisation vector. Each resulting period P ij is replaced by the closest discrete period in H to form a new matrix P . The value is saved into the vector ✏ and its index I min into I. The traversal does not consider rows of WCETs already saved into vectors V, I in previous iterations.

From the resulting error vector ✏, the max error e max is retrieved and the corresponding matrix indices (i, j) are retrieved. Since this error resulted from choosing a discrete period, we reset this error to zero by changing the utilisation.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENT SETUP
div.p: To estimate WCET using the MBPTA technique, 60 benchmarks from MiBench [14] and BEEBS [15] suites were selected. The benchmarks were statically linked and compiled with the arm linux eabi gcc compiler with -O0 optimisation flag. A total of 5000 taskset permutations and core affinities were generated. The hardware platform is an Odroid-XU4 board equipped with an ARM Big.Little Exynos 5422 chipset. The processor hosts two heterogeneous ARM A15 and A7 clusters of 4 cores each. The board was running LUbuntu 12.04 with the 3.10.y Linux kernel. Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) was disabled and both clusters set to run at their maximum speeds of 2GHz and 1.4GHz, respectively.

Since the perf tool supports recording performance counters from either the A15 or A7 clusters and not both, the Linux kernel was patched with PMCTrack patch [22]. PMCTrack is an open-source OS-oriented performance monitoring tool for GNU/Linux. For each of the 5000 tasksets, the tasks were assigned to their designated cores as per the core affinity distribution and the number of cycles of each task was logged separately for each cluster.

To estimate pWCET, MATLAB's Distribution Fitter toolbox was used. Both the Gumbel Distribution (EVT-Type I) and the Generalised EVT fits were used to analyse the execution times. Of the 60 tasks, 55 had a good fit, the others were discarded. For the remaining tasks, the probability density function of each was used to estimate the WCET. Similar to the approach taken in [20], and given the guidelines for safety assessment in airborne systems [23] which set the failure rate at 10 9 per hour of operation; the WCETs at probabilities [10 9 , 10 12 , 10 16 ] were considered. The lower the probability, the more pessimistic the estimation; yet the less probability of failure. In this paper, we consider WCETs at 10 16 probability.

A bounded discrete periods set H is generated given the technique in [6]. The exponents used to generate this taskset are 2 7 , 3 5 , 5 1 with an effective hyper-period of 155,520ms. To evaluate the performance of the CPA and PU algorithms, we created a test-bench which iterates over the total utilisation range of [0.1 0.95] in increments of 0.05. In each iteration, 100 random tasksets are generated for each taskset size in the range [4,55]. For the PU algorithm, the taskset size was capped at 10 due to high execution time. In total, around 90,000 taskset simulations were conducted. Statistical data were collected and the results reported in the next section.

div.head: V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
div.p: In Fig. 1, we compare how the resulting total utilisation from the CPA-AU, CPU-DU and PU algorithms deviates from the desired utilisation. The results are only shown for tasksets comprised of up to 10 tasks due to the O(n!) complexity of the PU algorithm. This limits timely analysis as the taskset size increases. Across the experiment space, our proposed algorithms are on average within 0.3% of the target utilisation. The PU algorithm errors hover between 3% -5%. Our algorithm outperforms the permutative algorithms by an order of magnitude due to the iterative utilisation adjustment phase which propagates and minimises the utilisation difference errors. Despite the exhaustive exploration which the PU algorithm performs, a better solution than that which our proposed solutions yield does not necessarily always exist. We observe that the minimum deviation errors of the PU algorithm were on average much higher than the average errors of our proposed algorithms. Fig. 2 shows the execution times of PU algorithms vs. the two versions of CPA. The execution time is independent of the desired utilisation. The O(n!) complexity of PU and the polynomial complexity of CPA algorithms is evident. In practice, the number of system tasks/threads is limited by the RTOS and by the nature of the real-time system. As such, our algorithms run in feasible time. Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 show the mean deviation errors across the broad system tasks size and utilisation space. Generally, both algorithms yield total utilisations within 0.5% of the target utilisation. CPA-DU yields slightly less errors on average when the taskset size is small (e.g. 4 -6 tasks ). However, both algorithms have increased errors when the number of tasks n increases and the total desired utilisation U is low (e.g. U = 0.1). This is easily explained by the fact that each task utilisation share is extremely small when the target utilisation is low. As such, tasks with execution times towards the higher end will have larger periods. In such scenario, two factors play into effect to increase the errors; the upper bound placed on the discrete period set, and the increased ratio between successive discrete periods. The former caps many periods at the maximum. In the latter case, the gap between a period and its replacement discrete period increases and therefore the errors. One solution to mitigate this issue is to increase the Hyper-Period time. Another is to explore a different set of discrete periods which has a larger number of periods. However, given the small number of embedded benchmarks available, and the less likelihood of having all task assigned to one core in a multi-core platform, the effects of such corner case are expected to diminish in practical considerations. In this paper, we have proposed a new methodology for preparing tasksets for evaluating real-time algorithms. Contrary to conventional approaches which algorithmically generate periods and task utilisations, compute WCETs and synthesise tasks through timed loops, our approach is practical. We select and compile binaries from real-time benchmarks and estimate their WCET through measurement based probabilistic timing analysis. We select the periods from a harmonic set of periods which have a bounded hyper-period. We introduce two algorithms; CPA-AU and CPA-DU which iterativley assign and adjust initial task utilisations. We compare the summed utilisation to the desired utilisation and we statistically analyse the performance of our algorithm. Compared to task utilisation assignment based on a permutative exploration, we show that our algorithms are time-efficient and have deviation errors at least an order of magnitude less than exhaustive algorithms.
